final_recommendation: The room converged on a fully operationalized $37M capital envelope with three staggered tranches ($15M stamper, $14M electronics, $8M labor/subsidy gap) tied to concrete triggers: month-12 supplier signals, month-16 tariff/RVC repricing, and month-18 joint-gate RVC certification failure. This transformed fragmented relocation/compliance risks into a priced, gated covenant package with conditional political-risk reserves.
key_conflicts: Initial fragmentation: relocation exposure and trade-credit risk treated as separate variables until supplier forced consolidation
Audit sequencing uncertainty: whether stamper and electronics suppliers faced joint-gate or sequential certification drove pricing debates until compliance clarified single joint-gate structure
Funding scope ambiguity: whether $27M covered capex-only or also subsidy gaps created covenant-stress uncertainty until CFO separated tranches
key_concessions: CFO conceded that initial $15M backstop covered only stampers, requiring second $14M electronics tranche
CFO acknowledged labor-cost headwind ($8-12M) as separate unfunded exposure, triggering third tranche commitment
Political-risk insurer conceded that 2026 RVC review (76% threshold) forces third supplier relocation ($12-18M), not just margin compression
All parties accepted month-18 joint-gate as single correlated default trigger rather than staggered failure scenario
red_lines: Month-18 RVC certification deadline: hard penalty trigger (25% tariffs retroactive, 30-50% order reductions) with no negotiable extension
Month-16 audit-prep window: supplier must file cert paperwork or credit stress becomes real
Month-12 forced-relocation decision point: models below 75% RVC lock capex sequencing constraint
Joint-gate structure: both stamper and electronics must pass month-18 audit or both models fail certification
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Supplier competitive shopping risk: 15-20% labor-cost headwind without subsidy cover could drive suppliers to competing OEMs (mentioned once by supplier, not priced)
Tariff-floor compression: tariff rates below 15% compress ROI by 40-60% but treated as repricing event rather than decision trigger
Covenant renegotiation possibility: month-16 deadline treated as hard constraint with no exploration of supplier debt restructuring alternatives
downstream_risk_variables: $37M capital envelope with three staggered tranches (month 12, 14, 16)
Month-18 joint-gate RVC certification as single correlated default trigger
Sedan and compact SUV models at 71-73% RVC requiring dual supplier relocation
Three stampers at 65-72% debt-to-EBITDA with $8-12M credit lines
Three electronics suppliers at 65-72% debt-to-EBITDA with $8-12M credit lines
25% ad-valorem tariff penalty ($18-22M annually per model) plus 30-50% order reduction on RVC failure

Month-12 subsidy-access trigger for third tranche drawdown
uncertainty_notes: 2026 USMCA review timing and scope remain uncertain—RVC threshold increase to 76% or tariff-floor changes could trigger third supplier relocation or reprice existing covenant triggers backward into month 16. Labor-cost headwind mitigation depends on suppliers' ability to access regional nearshoring subsidies, which is not yet confirmed. Supplier competitive shopping risk (switching to other OEMs under cost pressure) was surfaced but not quantified or priced into the trigger matrix.
